---
title: "Coming from Stata"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(tidystata)

entries <- tidystata:::findit_entries()

# Pandoc reads markdown inside HTML blocks, so encode ASCII punctuation as
# entities to keep code such as `x*` and quotes exactly as written. Non-ASCII
# text is encoded too: pkgdown may render in a non-UTF-8 locale, where cat()
# would print Chinese as <U+xxxx> escapes.
escape_html <- function(x) {
  vapply(
    x,
    function(text) {
      codes <- utf8ToInt(text)
      punct <- codes %in% c(33:47, 58:64, 91:96, 123:126) | codes > 127
      chars <- vapply(codes, intToUtf8, character(1))
      chars[punct] <- paste0("&#", codes[punct], ";")
      paste(chars, collapse = "")
    },
    character(1),
    USE.NAMES = FALSE
  )
}

section_tables <- function(section, task, detail, headers) {
  for (name in unique(entries[[section]])) {
    rows <- entries[entries[[section]] == name, ]
    notes <- ifelse(
      nzchar(rows[[detail]]),
      paste0(escape_html(rows[[task]]), "<br><small>", escape_html(rows[[detail]]), "</small>"),
      escape_html(rows[[task]])
    )
    table <- data.frame(
      paste0("<code>", escape_html(rows$stata), "</code>"),
      paste0("<code>", escape_html(rows$r), "</code>"),
      notes
    )
    names(table) <- escape_html(headers)
    cat("\n\n## ", escape_html(name), "\n\n", sep = "")
    cat(
      knitr::kable(table, format = "html", escape = FALSE, table.attr = 'class="table"'),
      sep = "\n"
    )
  }
}
```

[中文版](coming-from-stata-zh.html)

If you know Stata, you already know what you want to do; the question is how
to say it in R. This page lists Stata commands next to the R code that does the
same job, using tidystata where it has a Stata-style function and the standard
package everywhere else.

## Look it up from the console

`findit()` searches the same list from R. Type one Stata word bare, or quote
anything longer. Stata's abbreviations work.

```{r}
findit(reg)
findit("merge 1:1 id, keep(match)")
```

Call `findit()` with no argument for the whole list, or `??stata` to find this
help again.

## Where to find the rest

tidystata covers the everyday loop of inspecting, tabulating, summarising,
preparing and checking data. For everything else, these packages are the usual
choices:

- **Regression and fixed effects** (`regress`, `reghdfe`, `xtreg`,
  `ivregress`): `lm()` and `glm()`, or `fixest::feols()`.
- **Regression tables** (`esttab`, `outreg2`): `modelsummary::modelsummary()`.
- **Marginal effects** (`margins`): marginaleffects.
- **Reshaping** (`reshape`): `tidyr::pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()`.
- **Winsorising** (`winsor2`): `datawizard::winsorize()`.
- **Panels and calendar periods** (`tsset`, `xtset`, `L.`, `mofd()`): tsibble
  and lubridate.
- **Survey data** (`svyset`, `svy:`): srvyr and survey.
- **Graphs** (`twoway`, `histogram`): ggplot2; for `binscatter`, binsreg or
  `statar::stat_binmean()`.

tidystata and [statar](https://github.com/matthieugomez/statar) can be attached
together; only `tab()` and `xtile()` share names. Attach tidystata last, or write
`tidystata::tab()`.

A few RStudio habits replace Stata's interface: Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Return on a
Mac) runs the current line or selection, Tab completes names, and the
Environment and Files panes play the roles of Stata's Variables window and
`dir`.

In the tables below, `data` is your dataset, `data1` and `data2` are the master
and using data of a merge, and `fit` is a fitted model. Most entries use dplyr,
so attach it with `library(dplyr)` or `library(tidyverse)`.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
section_tables("section", "task", "detail", c("Stata", "R", "Notes"))
```

## R functions in this guide

R functions a Stata user is likely to meet, including every function used
above, with its package, a related Stata command and what it does. Type
`findit(name)`, such as `findit(left_join)`, to see the Stata commands it
replaces.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
functions <- tidystata:::findit_functions()
table <- data.frame(
  paste0("<code>", escape_html(functions$`function`), "()</code>"),
  escape_html(functions$package),
  escape_html(functions$stata),
  escape_html(functions[["description"]])
)
names(table) <- escape_html(c("Function", "Package", "Related Stata", "Description"))
cat(
  knitr::kable(table, format = "html", escape = FALSE, table.attr = 'class="table"'),
  sep = "\n"
)
```
